claims.text: Corrosion resistance in austenitic stainless steels is governed by the formation and stability of a chromium-rich surface oxide layer.
The chromium-rich oxide layer acts as a barrier to chloride-ion penetration.
Preventing chloride-ion penetration inhibits subsequent pit initiation.
The proposed initial material is passivated austenitic stainless steel, exemplified by 304L.
The controlled study will expose the steel to aqueous NaCl concentrations from 0.01 to 1.0 M at temperatures from 20 to 80°C.
The study will compare exposures with and without applied cathodic protection.
Chromium oxide layer thickness and composition are the proposed structural mediators.
The thickness and composition of the chromium oxide layer influence its protective properties.
A thicker and more uniform chromium oxide layer will produce higher corrosion resistance.
Higher corrosion resistance associated with a thicker and more uniform oxide layer will be observed as lower pit density.
Higher corrosion resistance associated with a thicker and more uniform oxide layer will be observed as a lower corrosion rate.
Increasing temperature will compromise chromium oxide layer stability.
Increasing chloride concentration will compromise chromium oxide layer stability.
Compromising chromium oxide layer stability will increase corrosion susceptibility.
Steel lacking a chromium oxide layer or having a compromised layer is the proposed baseline comparator.
The hypothesis is restricted to the tested chloride concentrations, temperatures, and steel compositions.
Surface roughness and contamination may independently influence corrosion resistance.
Finding no significant effect of the chromium oxide layer on corrosion resistance would falsify the hypothesis.
